window_text:
[3] John: Hi guys. Thanks for joining me and for having me.
[4] Jillian: Absolutely.
That’s Jillian Manus, from Structure Capital, introducing herself to today’s startup founder.
Alongside Jillian are 3 more investors, Phil Nadel from Forefront Venture Partners, Daniel Gulati with Comcast Ventures, and angel investor, and recent cryptocurrency poster child, James Altucher.
[5] A quick note: if you heard an earlier episode, Sandbox Commerce, and you’re wondering if we’ve heard back from James yet, the answer is no. But this pitch was recorded back in August of 2017.
Okay, on with the show.
Our investors are all here today to hear from John Renaldi, founder and CEO of today’s startup: Jiobit.
[6] Daniel: Jiobit?
[7] John: Jiobit. Like geolocation. And bit like small.
[8] Daniel: I know both. I'm familiar with both. That's great.
So they’ve got the name down. But behind a lot of truly great companies - and company names - is a personal story. And John’s is a doozy. Parents, brace yourselves.
[9] John: So about two years ago, almost exactly, my wife and I took our family to downtown Chicago. I'm from Chicago we showed up, oceans of people, of course. We go to a park, oceans of kids. Parents' nightmare, kids' dream. My wife and I split up. I took my son, my wife took my daughter. So, I had my son. I looked left or I can't tell you exactly how, but I think you guys, many of you have kids, probably a little bit older, but you remember when you just can't see them for a second. I look left, I look right, poof, Ethan is his name, he's gone. A couple of seconds turn into a couple of minutes. A couple of minutes turn to ten minutes.
[10] Jillian: Oh no.
[11] John: So I recruit parents. We’re running around, I’m telling them what he looks like, I have my phone out, I’m showing pictures. And thirty minutes later, I never found him. He found me.
[12] Daniel: How did he find you?
[13] John: I suspect he actually probably always saw sort of where he was. And I Just never saw him.
[14] Jillian: Children are so wily.
So fortunately John’s story had a happy ending — but it left an impression on him. He knew he never wanted to be in that position ever again.
[15] John: I came back from this and I bought every single type of tracking device I could possibly get my hands on.They're all just like terrible. Big bulky shoddy engineering, no innovation, no design. They lasted maybe a day if that. Every time I go to grab them they're out of power. And I thought, hey,I've always wanted to start my own business. And just never had the right idea. And so I pitched my wife the idea and she said, let's go do it.
So John set out to create a better way for parents to keep track of their kids. At the time, he was a Vice President at Motorola, so he knew how wireless chips worked — a technology he was able to customize for his own device. What he eventually came up with was Jiobit.
[16] John: It is the world's smallest and longest lasting smart tag. We call it a smart tag.
John is here today to ask investors for 750 thousand dollars to help bring his smart tag into the market. So what is this smart tag?
[17] John: And I can just show you, too. Always good to show and tell when you have a physical product. So this is Jiobit.
[18] Daniel: So you're pulling out what looks like a slightly bigger guitar pick like.
[19] John: Yeah, a little bit.
[20] Daniel: Head of an arrow is another way to put it. And it's the size of two quarters or something.
What our investors are struggling to describe is a small, plastic fob, about the size of a car’s keyless remote. It retails for 150 bucks. John shows investors an array of interchangeable attachments — loops and clips — that a parent can swap out to fasten the Jiobit to their kids’ backpack, shoelace, belt loop, whatever.
[21] Jillian: And you feel like you can clip it on to them so they're not going to take off that piece of clothing, so they're at school.
[22] John: So there's a childproof lock system, so similar to like you have a medicine bottle, where you have to have a certain amount of dexterity to actually remove it. we have a similar type of child lock mechanism.
Once the Jiobit is attached to their kid, a parent can track them through an app on their Smartphone. If their kid gets lost, like what happened to John in Chicago, a parent can immediately open up the app and find their kid.
According to John, this is the product parents have been waiting for.
[23] Jillian: So there are a lot of products out there. Okay, and I know quite a bit of them, in fact.There's everything from the basic which are Tiles, which people, people use Tiles on their children by the way.
[24] John: Yeah, they don't know that they don't work.
[25] Jillian: Well they do work, to tell you the truth. Actually a lot of them do work. So I'm just saying there's a lot on the market. So how do you distinguish yourself?
[26] Phil: Yeah, I agree with you. How is this product unique and different? What's the technology that makes it special?
[27] John: So uhh.. what we, our primary tech what we call is progressive beaconing.And what it does is really tries to solve the battery problem that so many consumer electronics have, particularly location products that just draw an amazing amount of battery. Which is why they only last about a day. Through this technology breakthrough, we can last up to 30 times longer than the best products on the market today.
[28] James: So 30 days.
[29] John: Up to 60 days.
[30] Jillian: But this is not your own battery? This is not your own IP?
[31] John: No, so the way the progressive beaconing works, it traverses all the different radio frequencies. It really has all the same tech that’s in your smartphone, but in something the size of about a quarter. So every radio that’s in your smartphone, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, cellular, GPS, all in our custom systems architecture.
The technology John calls progressive beaconing — patent pending — works by piggybacking on the cellular signal of your family’s phones. According to John, this allows it to use the least amount of battery possible, thus lasting weeks on end — way longer than any other geotracker currently on the market.
[32] Daniel: And so why do you need to conserve battery if the use case is a day trip with your children?
[33] John: Yeah. So what I found was every time, well, I have lots of things I charge in my house. Like, tablets, computers, phones. And so even though sometimes I would use it for day trips, but actually I was using it most every day, because they go to school, I never knew when this would happen. So I was putting it on them all the time.
[34] Phil: To Daniel's pointwhy not just charge it every night?
[35] John: So one thing that I found when I was using these products was that when I did go to use them every day or when I wanted to use them, they were always out of battery. I just forgot. And for us, having something that could just take out a little bit more anxiety in my day, make things just a little bit easier, and not have to worry about charging this thing all the time, made my life a lot easier for that.
[36] Daniel: okay.
The investors look a bit dubious. Sure, charging things is kind of a pain in the ass — but is it a big enough pain to build a whole company around?
[37] Daniel: it's a reasonably crowded landscape for these general beaconing devices. And so what's the differentiation here? Is it the core 30x longer technology? Is it the go-to-market?
[38] John: So software-wise, obviously mom and dad have a smartphone app. Software on the device itself. We use machine learning to employ different types of routes and behaviors and machines. So like a Nest thermostat. You don't really set it up, it just kind of learns what you do with it. Same here.
So Jiobit is more than just another geotracker with a longer-lasting battery. It’s also super
smart
.
[39] John: It learns where home is, it learns where school is, it learns the bus route. Tells you when you get to school, tells when you don't get to school.
[40] Jillian: Why is that important?
[41] John: Because I want to know when my child deviates from that routine. If they're taking the same path to school every day, I'm fine. Don't tell me any differently. But if they're not, that's when I want to know.
[42] Jillian: So it alerts you when they deviate?
[43] John: Correct. It will send me a push message right to my phone.
[44] Phil: Do any of the other products out there do that?
[45] John: No. Nope. So we....
[46] Jillian: So a phone does.
[47] John: Yeah of course.
[48] Jillian: So that is the other thing in terms of the age range here. Because people are giving their kids phones earlier to just keep in touch with them. Around ten years old. Some of them as early as eight years old.
[49] James: But the phone will track location, it won’t learn the route.
[50] Daniel: It just has a find my phone.
[51] Jillian: But it doesn’t learn.
[52] Phil: But how does this how does this differentiate if the child has a phone and you’re able to track them using the phone?
[53] Phil: I mean kids who are ten, eight, ten, I mean, I don't know, where I live they have phones. I don't know.
[54] John: So in more affluent neighborhoods you're right. On average though in the United States, definitely not.
[55] Jillian: And yet, but this is $150 to buy one of these things. So in an affluent... $150 is a lot for anybody to spend who is, as you said, not in the affluent neighborhoods,I mean, this is a lot.
[56] John: And exactly why we…
[57] Daniel: You could probably get a phone for $320 bucks a month.
[58] Jillian: Oh less. You can actually get less.
[59] John: Exactly why we want with scale. Bringing that down to the price points we talked about. We're obviously going to have higher costs right away. And you're totally right, as you scale, those are the price points you want to be at. A two-year-old, a three-year-old isn't going to have a smartphone, right. So you need to have something that's not a phone for those age groups.
So, yeah, kindergartners may not have cell phones. But, as investors are quick to point out: kids are getting phones earlier and earlier. In fact, a 2016 study by Research Central, pegged the average age for getting a first smartphone at 10, in 2012 that age was 12.
But this phone question may not even matter. The kid geotracking market is only one vertical — and John’s progressive beaconing technology might have infinite other possible uses.
[60] Daniel: I would argue that your progressive beaconing technology is actually way more powerful than any other vertical besides the one that you've chosen.
[61] John: Yeah. I mean we are...
[62] Daniel: Like let's take luggage, for example. Which is I can stick that, I can stick that device into my luggage, I never have to, I don't have to think about it on a trip and I can charge it when I get back home versus...
[63] John: Totally.
[64] Daniel: so why the initial focus on the kid problem when you could be solving a gazillion other problems?
[65] John: People that we, we did open up kind of a soft launch without really doing any marketing, and those pre-order people started hitting us up and they started buying it for pets. A pretty natural extension given that people that don't have kids but pets, many times treat them like children, or just as important. They're their most precious asset. And the battery life is obviously super important to those, because you don't want to go take it off your collar every 24 hours, right. So having something that lasts 30 days, 60 days is super important
[66] Daniel: why haven’t you, why don’t you guys just test ten form factors in ten verticals? Do pets, do kids. If it’s not that hard to change the form factor, put it all up on the site, spend six months really figuring it out. I Just worry that we’ve hit this local maximum around kids. We’ve anchored around kids because you had this experience, and obviously that’s important. But is there a 10x bigger business right next to us that we’re not seeing.
We’ve seen this before, sometimes investors get so captivated with an idea that they can’t help but imagine a whole new world of possibilities. Possibilities that appear to have a much bigger payout at the end of the rainbow.
But what happens when that pot of gold isn’t the same pot o’ gold the entrepreneur is going after
[67] John: For now, we're focused on two consumer markets. As we expand, these are things we'll definitely be looking at. But for the two consumer markets, I mean brand is just as important as tech. And building that out. So we are starting to invest in that.
[68] Daniel: We see so many companies where the founder, the founding team come in with this hypothesis on a vertical, and that hypothesis is just completely wrong. And there's actually this other vertical that's easily reachable and just kind of right next door that results in a much, much bigger business.
[69] Phil: You know granted it's born out of your traumatic experience, so you have an identity with that solution.
[70] Daniel: But that's not always the biggest business.
[71] Phil: That's what I'm saying. I'm saying you have to step back and look at the other use cases more analytically and not emotionally.
[72] John: I totally agree. And this is exactly the reason why we're launching pets in two weeks. And exactly why we're taking those conversations with those companies, to talk about and understand what their needs are, and we're coming to realize the same product can be used. We actually don't have to change the software
So John is willing to grow Jiobit beyond just the kids’ market. He’s just saying, one thing at a time. First kids, then pets, then who knows? Maybe luggage. But all in due time.
[73] Jillian: So have you launched this product yet?
[74] John: We have not. So we will ship it in a couple months.
[75] James: And what are you looking to raise and at what valuation?
[76] John: We raised $4.6 million already to really develop all the technology.
[77] James: You raised $4.6 million?
[78] John: Yes.
[79] Jillian: That’s a lot.
[80] James: What valuation?
[81] John: Ah, our post money is 13.
[82] Jillian: Wow. Okay, so this is pre, I mean you've no radar, you're pre-beta.
[83] John: We've been doing betas already on our first product. So this product here, we changed the design. So this has been in beta for some time.
[84] Jillian: What do your orders look like right now?
[85] John: So we haven't spent any marketing. We sold about $75,000 worth of inventory with monthly recurrings of $8,000.
[86] Jillian: Over what period of time?
[87] John: Like a week.
[88] Daniel: You've done $75,000 of sales in a week?
[89] John: Yeah.
[90] Jillian: So how much runway do you have off the 4.6?
[91] John: We’ll be... February.
[92] Jillian: Okay so you have until February until you run out of runway, Okay.
[93] John: And this would give us another 12 months.
[94] Daniel: Another 12 months.
So this funding John is asking for would buy him another year to get Jiobit off the ground. And even though Jillian seemed a bit shocked by the company’s 13 million dollar valuation, the investors were all impressed by the 75K in preorders John brought in in just one week.
Has he managed to convince them that Jiobit’s revolutionary technology is worth the hefty price?
Here’s Daniel
[95] Daniel: Almost all of our successful portfolio companies have started with a really deep founder pain point. A really personal founder pain point. And that doesn't guarantee success, but I think it's kind of a necessary condition right.And I definitely, I mean, the way, you didn't walk in and pitch this as a hardware startup. You pitched it as a solution to a problem that you had. And I think that is really compelling, and I think you are really compelling. I think this is a market and a space with just lots of competing substitutes. Whether aaa it's subderm chips, whether it's aaa smartphones You have this sea of substitution that could happen here. And so that's a big worry for me, frankly. And then the last piece I think about it is just ownership for the fund. So if you're raising 700k on a $15 million valuation, it's just not going to get us the VC ownership that we need to move the needle. And so despite what I said about you being an absolutely compelling founder, just for those reasons I'm going to have to pass
With Daniel out, it’s on to Phil
[96] Phil: I just want to jump in and say, for me, I think the tech is really cool. There are a whole bunch of opportunities here. You really seem to have your stuff together and know what you're talking about, and it looks like you've assembled a great team. For me, it's a little too early. I'd want to see it further developed into certain use cases where you're showing some traction, getting some actual orders, which sounds like it's very soon.So for me, I'm a pass. I think you're off to a great start and I wish you all the best.
Phil’s out, here’s James.
[97] James: So I’m sort of in line with everybody here. But I think, to Daniel’s point, I think it’s okay if you go out with any use case and you’ll sort of figure it out as you go along. Like that will kind of evolve with just your incoming phone calls and you’ll be surprised and we’ll all be surprised, six months you’ll be, you know, the luggage company, or the construction company, or the API company. Something will happen. Many companies pivot and find their right spot with their technology.for me, I’m, they’re venture capitalists, I’m an angel investor, so the valuation puts me out right away. I think for you, a great return on this is if you close this round, you show some use cases, Motorola or Google or whoever comes along and buys you for $80 million and you become a very wealthy man and we make 5x our money is not as interesting to me. So I have to pass for that — but I do think you’re going to end up doing well with this.
Three of four investors are out, now it’s up to Jillian
[98] Jillian: Um, I have to be honest with you. I have been actually completely schizophrenic on this one. Because half of me is saying, for all the reasons Daniel has ticked off, this just doesn't make sense. One of the biggest problems for me is the, yes, the competitive landscape, I know a bit about but I'm going to have to know more of, because I don't know your technology well enough, and so I can't really assess it right in this immediate moment and juxtapose it to everything out there, including Revolar and the other ones. This would take more a dive for me. I love this. I love the why on this. Okay. We, our most precious, precious cargo, our most precious possession are our children. Anything to make them more safe. That said, I am going to pass
[thank yous]
[99] Jillian: It was really great to meet you. I love your energy, by the way. I love your smile. I love your determination. And I’m glad you found Ethan. Absolutely. Absolutely.
decision_quote:
Um, I have to be honest with you. I have been actually completely schizophrenic on this one. Because half of me is saying, for all the reasons Daniel has ticked off, this just doesn't make sense. One of the biggest problems for me is the, yes, the competitive landscape, I know a bit about but I'm going to have to know more of, because I don't know your technology well enough, and so I can't really assess it right in this immediate moment and juxtapose it to everything out there, including Revolar and the other ones. This would take more a dive for me. I love this. I love the why on this. Okay. We, our most precious, precious cargo, our most precious possession are our children. Anything to make them more safe. That said, I am going to pass
[thank yous]

taxonomy.label: business_model_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the startup’s revenue model, monetization approach, or service/automation mix as a driver of business viability.

taxonomy.label: business_viability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's concern that the overall business viability, model, or economics are not sufficiently compelling.

taxonomy.label: capital_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the startup will require substantial ongoing capital investment, increasing risk or misalignment with the investor’s funding capacity.

taxonomy.label: competitive_advantage_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s beliefs about what drives defensibility or sustainable competitive advantage in a market.

taxonomy.label: competitive_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the category is highly competitive, attention‐constrained, and requires heavy marketing to win, reducing the likelihood of outsized success.

taxonomy.label: competitive_landscape_inertia
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the difficulty of displacing or changing behavior of incumbents due to entrenched solutions, habits, or workflows.

taxonomy.label: deal_terms_complexity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the structure or details of deal terms (e.g., convertibles, SAFEs, preferred terms) may introduce complexity, ambiguity, or unfavorable outcomes.

taxonomy.label: decision_context_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints imposed by the specific evaluation format, environment, or context rather than the startup's fundamentals.

taxonomy.label: dilution_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the financing plan will cause excessive dilution relative to their ownership goals or stage fit.

taxonomy.label: execution_risk_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the team may not yet have demonstrated sufficient execution reliability or maturity for the risk level of the round.

taxonomy.label: founder_equity_incentive_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to ensuring founders retain sufficient ownership to remain properly motivated, aligned, and incentivized for the long-term company‐building journey.

taxonomy.label: founder_execution
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of the founders' execution ability, resourcefulness, pace, and operational grit.

taxonomy.label: founder_market_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales based on how well the founder's background, experience, or motivation aligns with the target market.

taxonomy.label: founder_qualities
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the founders' personal traits, capabilities, or appeal.

taxonomy.label: founder_skillset
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the founder's core skills or functional strengths relevant to company-building.

taxonomy.label: fund_economics_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor’s fund size, check size, or ownership goals that constrain how selective they must be when choosing investments.

taxonomy.label: fundraising_demand_signal
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the company will attract capital easily due to current or expected investor demand.

taxonomy.label: growth_projection_risk
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the company’s growth, revenue, or user‐scale projections are insufficiently modeled, unrealistic, or lack credible underlying assumptions.

taxonomy.label: investment_thesis_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's predefined investment thesis or mandate that restricts them to specific sectors, business models, or company types.

taxonomy.label: investment_upside_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's view that the risk‐reward profile offers disproportionately large potential returns relative to downside risk.

taxonomy.label: investor_domain_knowledge_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor lacking the necessary domain knowledge to effectively assess the technology, moat, competition, or overall viability of the opportunity.

taxonomy.label: investor_experience_bias
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's prior personal experiences, wins, losses, or operational history that shape their judgment of a new opportunity.

taxonomy.label: market_entry_path_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that there is a clear, reachable initial customer segment that can serve as an effective wedge into the larger market.

taxonomy.label: market_problem_validation
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor perceiving the underlying problem as real, important, or painful enough to support a venture-scale solution.

taxonomy.label: market_size_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s belief about the absolute or relative size and fluidity of the addressable market.

taxonomy.label: market_timing
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the timing is favorable or unfavorable for this market, category, or product to emerge or scale.

taxonomy.label: mission_alignment_preference
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's personal or emotional alignment with the startup's mission or purpose.

taxonomy.label: portfolio_conflict_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints arising from existing portfolio investments that create competitive conflicts preventing a new investment.

taxonomy.label: product_adoption
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to evidence that end users are adopting and using the product meaningfully.

taxonomy.label: product_appeal_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s positive perception of the product’s appeal, quality, or desirability based on their own reaction.

taxonomy.label: product_differentiation_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to how unique, defensible, or hard-to-copy the product or technology is perceived to be.

taxonomy.label: product_success_factor_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to which product components or attributes are perceived as most essential to the startup's ability to succeed.

taxonomy.label: solution_feasibility_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the proposed product or solution is technically or operationally feasible.

taxonomy.label: stage_valuation_mismatch
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of a mismatch between the company’s stage of progress and the valuation being requested.

taxonomy.label: traction_repeatability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that current traction, usage, or revenue signals are too early or insufficiently repeatable to support scaling.

taxonomy.label: unit_economics_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the business benefits from structurally attractive unit economics, such as profitable or self-reinforcing customer acquisition.

taxonomy.label: venture_scale_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the companys market dynamics, ceiling, or competitive landscape limit its ability to achieve venture-scale outcomes.

taxonomy.label: investor_value_add_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the investor can contribute meaningful help, networks, or domain value beyond capital to this specific company.

taxonomy.label: founder_coachability_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how receptive the founder is to feedback, advice, or course-correction and their ability to read and respond to the room.

taxonomy.label: founder_communication_quality
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the founder's clarity, articulation, command of their numbers, and storytelling ability when presenting the business.

taxonomy.label: founder_motivation_authenticity
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the genuineness, personal connection, or origin of the founder's drive to work on this particular problem.

taxonomy.label: go_to_market_strategy_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how the company will reach and acquire customers, including sales motion, channel scalability, and cost of acquisition.

taxonomy.label: founder_investor_vision_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the founder's intended direction or focus for the company aligns with the path the investor believes in or would back.

taxonomy.label: corporate_structure_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the company's legal entity, incorporation, jurisdiction, or IP-ownership structure as a barrier or condition to investing.
